## Introduction

An ordination plot can suggest that groups of samples differ. ecodive's
permutation tests check whether the difference is real: does a variable,
such as treatment or body site, explain the distances between samples?

Each test takes a distance matrix (`dm`) from any beta diversity metric,
plus the variable to test: either a vector with one value per sample, or
the name of a column in a data frame of sample metadata (`data`).

| Function      | Test                                              | Variable    | Question                                                      |
| :------------ | :------------------------------------------------ | :---------- | :------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `permanova()` | Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance   | either      | Do group centroids differ? How much variance (R²) does it explain? |
| `permdisp()`  | Homogeneity of Multivariate Dispersions           | categorical | Do groups differ in their spread?                             |
| `anosim()`    | Analysis of Similarities                          | categorical | Are distances within groups smaller than between them (ranks)? |
| `mrpp()`      | Multi-Response Permutation Procedure              | categorical | Are distances within groups smaller than expected?            |
| `mantel()`    | Mantel Test                                       | numeric     | Do distances correlate with differences in a numeric variable, or with another distance matrix? |
| `mantel_partial()` | Partial Mantel Test                          | numeric     | Do they still, after removing the effect of a third distance matrix? |

They give the same statistics as `vegan`'s `adonis2()`, `betadisper()`,
`anosim()`, `mrpp()`, `mantel()`, and `mantel.partial()`, with permutations
run in parallel C, and the p-values are identical for any number of
threads.

The examples use R's built-in `iris` data, as in `vignette('ordination')`:
150 flowers, four measurements each, and three species.

```{r}
library(ecodive)

dm <- bray(iris[, 1:4])
```


## PERMANOVA

`permanova()` is the most widely used test. Give the grouping variable as a
column name of `data`, or as a vector.

```{r}
permanova(dm, 'Species', iris)
```

Species explain most of the variation between flowers (`R2`), and no
permutation of the labels did as well (`p`). The p-value cannot be smaller
than 1 / (`permutations` + 1), so use more permutations for a more precise
one.

A `formula` tests several variables at once. `by = 'terms'` tests each in
turn, as `adonis2()` does, and `strata` restricts permutations to within
blocks (such as subjects in a repeated-measures design).

```{r}
permanova(dm, data = iris, formula = ~ Species + Sepal.Width, by = 'terms')
```


## Checking the spread

PERMANOVA can also give a small p-value when groups have the same center
but different spreads. `permdisp()` tests the spread on its own; a
significant result means a PERMANOVA difference may come partly or wholly
from dispersion.

```{r}
permdisp(dm, 'Species', iris)
```

Here the three species are equally spread, so the PERMANOVA result above
reflects a real difference in their centers. The warning comes from
Bray-Curtis distances not being Euclidean: a flower can then sit at a
negative squared distance from its species' center, which `permdisp()`
sets to zero (Anderson 2006).


## ANOSIM and MRPP

`anosim()` compares the ranks of distances within and between groups. `R`
near 1 means every group is distinct, and near 0 means no difference.
`mrpp()` compares the average distance within groups with what random
groups would give.

```{r}
anosim(dm, 'Species', iris)

mrpp(dm, 'Species', iris)
```


## Pairwise comparisons

When an overall test finds that the groups differ, the next question is
usually which ones. `pairwise = TRUE` reruns the test on each pair of
groups' samples, and adjusts the pairs' p-values for multiple testing
(Holm's method by default; `p_adjust = 'BH'` controls the false discovery
rate instead). The overall result is unchanged.

```{r}
res <- permanova(dm, 'Species', iris, pairwise = TRUE)
res$pairwise
```

`p_value` is each pair's own permutation p-value, and `p_adjusted` the
value to report. `anosim()` and `mrpp()` take the same arguments, and
`permdisp()` adds adjusted p-values to its pairwise t tests:

```{r}
permdisp(dm, 'Species', iris, pairwise = TRUE)$pairwise
```


## Mantel test

`mantel()` correlates `dm` with a numeric variable, or with a second
distance matrix: here, whether flowers with similar petals also have
similar sepals. `method` can be `'pearson'`, `'spearman'`, or `'kendall'`.

```{r}
sepals <- bray(iris[, 1:2])
petals <- bray(iris[, 3:4])

mantel(sepals, petals, method = 'spearman')
```

`mantel_partial()` removes the effect of a third set of distances, `given`:
here, whether sepals and petals still match after accounting for petal
width alone.

```{r}
mantel_partial(sepals, petals, given = 'Petal.Width', data = iris, method = 'spearman')
```


## Running tests by name

`dist_test()` runs any test by name, as `dist_ord()` does for ordinations.
It checks that the variable suits the test (categorical or numeric), and
names are matched forgivingly: `'adonis2'` finds `permanova` and
`'betadisper'` finds `permdisp`.

```{r}
dist_test(dm, 'adonis2', 'Species', iris)
```

Each result converts to a one-row data frame with the same columns, so
several tests combine into one table.

```{r}
tests <- list_dist_tests(val = 'id', groups = 'categorical')

do.call(rbind, lapply(tests, function (test)
  as.data.frame(dist_test(dm, test, 'Species', iris)) ))
```


## Reproducibility

Permutations come from ecodive's own random number generator, set by
`seed` (default `0`), so the same call always gives the same p-value, on
any computer and with any number of `cpus`. R's `set.seed()` has no effect.

```{r}
identical(
  permanova(dm, 'Species', iris, seed = 1, cpus = 1),
  permanova(dm, 'Species', iris, seed = 1, cpus = 2) )
```
